title: System design
description: Caching, queues, consistency, scaling, reliability and API patterns you meet in real backends.

cards.question: In the cache-aside pattern, who loads data into the cache after a miss?
cards.explanation: With cache-aside (lazy loading), the app checks the cache, reads the database on a miss, then writes the result into the cache.

cards.question: A write-through cache updates the cache and the backing store as part of the same write.
cards.explanation: Write-through keeps the cache in step with the store on every write, at the cost of slower writes. Write-back defers the store write.

cards.question: Without explicit invalidation, what does a TTL on a cache entry put an upper bound on?
options: How long a stale entry can be served
cards.explanation: An entry expires after its TTL, so even if nobody invalidates it, stale data is served for at most that long.

cards.question: A hot key expires and many requests miss at once, all hitting the database. What is this called?
cards.explanation: A stampede (thundering herd) happens when many callers rebuild the same entry at once. Locks, request coalescing or early refresh help.

cards.question: Adding random jitter to cache TTLs makes stampedes more likely.
cards.explanation: Jitter spreads expirations out, so many keys written together do not all expire at the same moment and hit the database together.

cards.question: With at-least-once delivery, what must a consumer be ready to handle?
cards.explanation: At-least-once means a message is redelivered if the ack is lost or late, so the same message can arrive more than once.

cards.question: An idempotent operation has the same effect whether it runs once or several times.
cards.explanation: Idempotency makes retries and duplicate deliveries safe. A common technique is to record a unique key per request and skip repeats.

cards.question: What is a dead-letter queue for?
cards.explanation: After a message fails a set number of times, it moves to a dead-letter queue so it stops blocking work and can be inspected.

cards.question: Producers outpace consumers. Which mechanism signals producers to slow down?
cards.explanation: Backpressure pushes load limits upstream, for example with bounded queues that block or reject, so memory does not grow without limit.

cards.question: If a broker guarantees at-least-once delivery, exactly-once processing comes for free.
cards.explanation: At-least-once allows redelivery. Effectively-once processing needs idempotent consumers or deduplication on your side.

cards.question: What does a B-tree index on a column mainly speed up?
options: Lookups and range scans on it
cards.explanation: A B-tree keeps keys sorted, so equality lookups and range queries on that column avoid a full table scan.

cards.question: Each index you add makes inserts and updates on that table a bit slower.
cards.explanation: Every write must also update each affected index, so indexes trade write speed and storage for faster reads.

cards.question: You write to the primary, then read at once from an async replica. What might you get?
cards.explanation: Async replicas apply changes after a delay (replication lag), so a read right after a write can miss it. Read-your-writes needs routing care.

cards.question: Per the CAP theorem, during a network partition a system must trade off which two?
cards.explanation: When nodes cannot talk, a system either rejects some requests to stay consistent or answers them and risks returning stale data.

cards.question: In ACID, isolation is the property that a committed transaction survives a crash.
cards.explanation: That is durability. Isolation means concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work, as set by the isolation level.

cards.question: Adding more servers behind a load balancer is called what?
cards.explanation: Horizontal scaling adds machines. Vertical scaling gives one machine more CPU or memory, which is simpler but hits a ceiling.

cards.question: Horizontal scaling is easier when app servers are stateless.
cards.explanation: If session and state live in a shared store, any server can handle any request, so you can add or remove servers freely.

cards.question: Why shard by a hash of the user ID?
options: It spreads users evenly across shards
It removes the need for backups
It keeps all data on one node
cards.explanation: Hashing spreads keys evenly and avoids hot ranges. The cost is that queries across many users must fan out to many shards.

cards.question: When you add a node, what does consistent hashing reduce compared with `hash % N`?
cards.explanation: With `hash % N`, changing N remaps most keys. Consistent hashing moves only roughly 1/N of the keys to the new node.

cards.question: Sticky sessions let a load balancer send each request to any server it likes.
cards.explanation: Sticky sessions pin a client to one server. That keeps local state usable but makes balancing uneven and failover harder.

cards.question: Why add random jitter to exponential retry backoff?
options: To stop clients retrying in sync
cards.explanation: Without jitter, clients that failed together retry together and hammer the recovering service in waves. Jitter spreads them out.

cards.question: A network call to another service with no timeout can tie up a worker indefinitely.
cards.explanation: A hung peer holds threads or connections forever, which can exhaust pools and spread the outage. Always set timeouts.

cards.question: What does a circuit breaker do while it is open?
cards.explanation: After repeated failures the breaker opens and rejects calls at once, giving the dependency time to recover. Later it lets a trial call through.

cards.question: Which rate-limiting algorithm allows short bursts while enforcing an average rate?
cards.explanation: Tokens refill at a steady rate up to a bucket size. Saved tokens allow a burst, but the long-run rate cannot exceed the refill rate.

cards.question: It is always safe to auto-retry a payment POST that timed out.
cards.explanation: The first attempt may have succeeded before the timeout, so a retry can charge twice. Use an idempotency key so the server can dedupe.

cards.question: Why prefer cursor pagination over offset pagination for large, changing lists?
options: It allows jumping to page N
Stable pages and fast deep paging
It returns all rows at once
cards.explanation: A cursor resumes after the last seen key, so inserts do not shift pages and the database seeks instead of skipping many rows.

cards.question: In HTTP, PUT and DELETE are defined as idempotent, but POST is not.
cards.explanation: Repeating a PUT or DELETE leaves the server in the same state. POST may create a new resource each time, so retries need care.

cards.question: Which HTTP status code tells a client it is sending too many requests?
cards.explanation: 429 Too Many Requests signals rate limiting, often with a Retry-After header. 503 means the service is unavailable.

cards.question: Which change breaks existing API clients?
cards.explanation: Clients may read the removed field and fail. Additive, optional changes are usually backward compatible; removals need a new version.

cards.question: gRPC runs over HTTP/2 and uses Protocol Buffers by default.
cards.explanation: gRPC is an RPC framework: you define services in .proto files and get typed client and server stubs, unlike resource-oriented REST.
